title: Fatality inquiry hears woman had high levels of drugs and sedatives in her system
article: The combination of alcohol and extremely high levels of prescription painkillers and sedatives found in a woman who died in an RCMP holding cell last year was sufficient to cause death, Alberta's chief toxicologist testified Thursday.

Colleen Marie Akazay, 25, was found unresponsive in a Grande Prairie RCMP detachment holding cell about seven hours after she was arrested and lodged in cells for public intoxication on Feb. 18, 2006.
Twenty-one months later, the circumstances of her death - and the days and weeks leading up to it - were made public at the first day of her fatality inquiry in Grande Prairie.

Prescription records presented revealed that, in the six weeks prior to her death, Akazay had been prescribed 180 tablets of the sedative bromazepam. That quantity, Alberta's chief toxicologist Graham Jones pointed out, is a four- to six-month supply under normal circumstances.
The toxicology report, prepared by Jones, showed that Akazay had consumed at least five tablets of the drug shortly before her death. A normal dosage is one or one-and-a-half tablets.
The concentration of codeine, a painkiller, found in Akazay's blood was nearly twice as high as what is normally considered a lethal concentration, Jones said.

He added that, in his conservative estimate, Akazay would have had to consume at least five or six tablets of Tylenol 4, or 10 to 12 tablets of Tylenol 3, shortly before her death to have a codeine concentration that high.
Jones said the high concentrations of codeine can lead to fatal respiratory complications.

"It will dull the brain's ability to sense the build-up of carbon dioxide," he said, adding that the person "will not breathe as efficiently or as fast as a normal person," and that, in essence, the brain will not get enough oxygen, which can lead to brain damage or death.
Others who took the stand Thursday provided details on Akazay's activities before her arrest and incarceration.

According to Cpl. Geordie Simpson, the lead RCMP investigator in the case, Akazay and her common-law husband came to Grande Prairie from Grimshaw on Feb. 16, 2006 and spent the night at the Oasis warming shelter downtown.
The next morning, Akazay had a dentist appointment, where, after getting some work done, she was prescribed some Tylenol 3 tablets and ibuprofen.

Soon after, Simpson continued, the couple made their way to a bar at a downtown hotel where, after staff saw the intoxicated woman vomit on herself and foam coming from the mouth, she was asked to leave.
Around 9 p.m. the couple returned to the hotel and continued drinking and stayed until about 2:30 a.m. before leaving to spend another night at the Oasis shelter.

However, a security guard enforcing the midnight cut-off for checking in at the shelter told the two they could not enter the shelter. When the couple came back, police were called and Akazay and her companion were arrested for public intoxication.

"She was so drunk she couldn't keep her eyes open ... she was falling asleep on the toilet," Dorileen Horseman, who was Akazay's cellmate that night, told court Thursday. "I remember thinking that they should be taking her to the hospital or something."
Horseman added Akazay was exhibiting signs consistent with someone suffering from a drug overdose, and she got the woman she described as "incoherent" some water and helped her into bed.
Akazay fell asleep immediately, Horseman said, and was snoring so loudly Horseman asked to be moved to the next cell.
Though she remembers waking up throughout the night and hearing the snoring, Horseman said she recalled the time she woke up and no sound was coming out of Akazay's cell.
"I didn't hear anything ... I thought she was released," Horseman said.
But, at 10:47 a.m., when Sgt. Ross Gear attempted to wake Akazay to release her, she had no pulse and her body was cold, Simpson said.
After an unsuccessful attempt by medical staff to revive her, she was pronounced dead.

In addition to the prescription drugs, Jones testified Akazay had a blood-alcohol concentration nearly half that of the legal limit and he found evidence Akazay had used cocaine in the 24-hour period leading up to her death, though that did not factor into her death.

Jones testified a small amount of methadone - a painkiller often used to help people withdraw from heroin and morphine - was also found in Akazay's system and "may have had a minor contributory effect," in her death.
Simpson testified when Akazay was lodged in cells, among her belongings were six pill bottles.
There were four with labels dated Feb. 15, 2006, another dated Feb. 17, 2006 and one dated Dec. 2, 2005.

Though most bottles were only missing pills that would have been consistent with prescribed usage, the 20-tablet bottle of Tylenol 3s she was prescribed less than 24 hours before her death had only two tablets left.
In her jacket, police found a small plastic bag with some white powder and various Tylenol 4 tablets.

A friend who saw Akazay only hours before she was arrested said she saw Akazay dip her fingers into the powder bag - which she said appeared to be more full than in the police pictures - and touch her finger to her tongue.
The fatality inquiry will continue today.
More police and civilian witnesses are expected to testify before Grande Prairie provincial court Judge Jim Watson.
Public inquiries held under the Fatality Inquiries Act are limited to establishing the cause, manner, time, place and circumstances of death, as well as the identity of the deceased.
The judge may make recommendations on the prevention of similar occurrences but is prohibited, under the act, from making findings of legal responsibility or assigning blame.
Fatality inquiries are scheduled after all investigations have been completed.
